hearby.title: HearBy
hearby.summary: An app that turns sound into visuals, so deaf and hard-of-hearing people can see what words alone don't carry: tone, emotion, pitch, rhythm and the sound around them. Built by team Detrio at the AT&T Hackathon Junior 2026.

sections.heading: The brief
sections.text: Subtitles show what was said, not how. We wanted to show the rest — whether a voice rises or falls, speeds up, gets louder or goes quiet — for deaf people, for people who struggle to read tone, and for anyone training their own voice.

sections.heading: The process
sections.text: We brainstormed and mapped the idea out in FigJam, then built a sound engine that breaks any audio into the eight elements of music: pitch, rhythm, dynamics, timbre, harmony, articulation, texture and form. It also tells speech from music and noise, and is ready for several microphones to find where a sound comes from. A debug page showing the live numbers came first; the app was designed around it — intro, legend, customisation, a camera overlay and live subtitles.

sections.heading: The outcome
sections.text: HearBy runs as a native macOS app and an Android app from one codebase, analysing 20 seconds of audio in about one second. Voice becomes a live line you can read at a glance, with subtitles underneath and the option to record it.

predichess.title: Predichess
predichess.summary: A web app for building and playing interactive chess lessons. Authors put lessons together from board positions, text and questions; players work through them and earn XP and Elo.

sections.heading: The brief
sections.text: Chess lessons online are mostly videos you watch, not something you do. Predichess makes every lesson a sequence of positions and questions, so the player has to think through each move instead of just following along.

sections.heading: The process
sections.text: Three parts: Learn, to browse community lessons and step through them; an Editor, to build lessons from tasks and steps, save drafts and publish them with a difficulty; and Home, with your profile, Elo, XP and where you left off. It first ran on an Express server with Prisma and MariaDB.

sections.heading: The outcome
sections.text: A live demo on GitHub Pages that runs entirely in the browser: a small built-in backend answers the same API routes as the original server and keeps accounts, lessons and progress in local storage. Every push is tested, built and published automatically.

graphite.title: Graphite
graphite.summary: My own second-brain note app: a Zettelkasten that keeps every note as a plain Markdown file in a folder you own, and runs on macOS, Windows, Linux and Android from one codebase.

sections.heading: The brief
sections.text: I wanted the learning setup I'd built in Obsidian without the plugins and the busywork: notes that link to each other, move from capture to processed to kept, and turn into flashcards I actually review. No accounts, no lock-in — just .md files in my own Drive folder.

sections.heading: The process
sections.text: A desktop and mobile app built with Tauri, React and CodeMirror, with the heavy lifting — loading the vault, search, stats, scanning music and video — moved into Rust. Wikilinks with backlinks, a graph of every note, version history, GitHub sync, and a design-token theme system where every colour can be edited in Settings.

sections.heading: The outcome
sections.text: An app I use every day, shipping updates that install over the old build and keep notes and settings. Flashcards are scheduled with FSRS, and experimental spaces for training, music and video grow on the same notes-and-tags foundation.
